citation: Møller JE, Engstrøm T, Jensen LO, Eiskjær H, Mangner N, Polzin A, et al. Microaxial Flow Pump or Standard Care in Infarct-Related Cardiogenic Shock. N Engl J Med. 2024;390:1382-1393
one_liner: Routine Impella CP reduced 180-day mortality (45.8% vs 58.5%) but increased severe bleeding (20.1% vs 3.4%) and renal-replacement therapy (41.9% vs 26.7%) in selected infarct-related cardiogenic shock.

pico.population: Adults with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction and cardiogenic shock (systolic BP <100 mmHg or vasopressor/inotrope, arterial lactate ≥2.5 mmol/L, LVEF <45%)
pico.intervention: Routine microaxial flow pump (Impella CP) placement plus standard care
pico.comparison: Standard care alone (guideline-concordant shock care, with rescue MCS at discretion)

background.existing_knowledge: Infarct-related cardiogenic shock remains a high-mortality syndrome despite rapid reperfusion and modern intensive care. Temporary mechanical circulatory support devices are widely used but prior evidence was dominated by observational studies and small trials, with concerns about bleeding and vascular complications.
background.knowledge_gap: Equipoise persisted regarding whether routine early left ventricular unloading/support improves survival or simply shifts morbidity.
background.hypothesis: Routine microaxial flow pump support plus standard care reduces all-cause mortality at 180 days compared with standard care alone.

methods.design: International, multicentre, randomised, open-label, parallel-group trial with 1:1 allocation, stratified by site, intention-to-treat analysis.
methods.setting: High-volume tertiary centres in Denmark and Germany with 24/7 invasive cardiology and critical care.

inclusion: Cardiogenic shock defined by systolic BP <100 mmHg (or vasopressor/inotrope) and arterial lactate ≥2.5 mmol/L and LVEF <45%
exclusion: Severe peripheral vascular disease precluding large-bore access
Other conditions limiting feasibility/safety of device placement

methods.intervention: Routine Impella CP placement after randomisation (typically before PCI completion), run at highest performance level, goal support ≥48 hours, managed in specialised cardiac ICU with protocolised weaning.
methods.comparison: Standard care: guideline-concordant shock care, revascularisation, vasopressors/inotropes, ventilation, and escalation to other MCS (IABP, VA-ECMO) at clinician discretion.
methods.blinding: Open-label (device strategy not amenable to blinding); primary outcome (all-cause death) objective.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned to detect 18% absolute mortality reduction (60% to 42%) with 80% power, two-sided α=0.05; target 360 patients (162 per group) to accommodate dropouts; one interim analysis after 180 patients with stopping boundary P≤0.001.
secondary_outcomes: Composite of major adverse clinical events
Days alive and out of hospital at 180 days
Composite safety endpoint (severe bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis, device failure, worsening aortic regurgitation)
methods.follow_up: 180 days (primary), with in-hospital and 30-day outcomes reported.

headline_bullets: Mortality was lower with Impella CP at 180 days (45.8% vs 58.5%; HR 0.74; 95% CI 0.55–0.99; P=0.04).
Device strategy increased major harms: severe bleeding (20.1% vs 3.4%) and renal-replacement therapy (41.9% vs 26.7%).
Protocol separation was substantial: Impella CP placed in 95.0% vs 1.7% crossover.

outcomes_table.note: Composite of major adverse clinical events (trial-defined)

outcomes_table.outcome: Days alive and out of hospital (180 days)

outcomes_table.note: Severe bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis, device failure, or worsening aortic regurgitation
Clinically important excess organ support requirement
Low absolute numbers; wide confidence interval

domains.notes: 1:1 randomisation stratified by site; central randomisation; independent DSMC.
Open-label design; primary outcome (all-cause death) objective, reducing detection bias; co-intervention differences possible.
360 randomised, 5 excluded post-randomisation due to consent issues (1 Impella, 4 control), leaving 179 vs 176 analysed; ITT analysis.
Impella CP placed in 95.0% of intervention group; 5.0% did not receive device; crossover in control group 1.7% received Impella CP, plus 4 received as unloading during VA-ECMO.
Age 67 vs 68 years; lactate 3.3 vs 3.4 mmol/L; SBP 80 vs 80 mm Hg; LVEF 29% vs 30%.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall, internal validity appears moderate-to-strong given robust randomisation, minimal crossover, and an objective primary outcome; limitations include open-label co-intervention potential and small post-randomisation exclusions related to consent.

domains.notes: Highly selected population; among 1211 screened, 851 excluded, with coma after OHCA a common exclusion (435 patients).

Requires immediate access to large-bore arterial cannulation, catheter lab workflows, and capability to manage bleeding/vascular complications and renal failure; applies to STEMI-related shock with predominant LV failure, not to comatose post-arrest or RV failure.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is moderate-to-limited: results most applicable to carefully selected infarct-related cardiogenic shock patients in experienced, high-resource centres with established shock pathways.

strengths: Large pragmatic randomised trial in a high-mortality condition
Strong protocol separation (95.0% vs 1.7% microaxial pump placement)
limitations: Open-label design with potential co-intervention imbalance
Substantial exclusions during screening (notably coma after OHCA)
Post-randomisation exclusions due to consent issues
High rate of major device-related complications
Recruitment over many years with evolving practice patterns

critical_appraisal.summary: DanGer Shock is a well-conducted RCT demonstrating a mortality benefit with Impella CP in selected STEMI-related cardiogenic shock, but the benefit is accompanied by a substantial increase in major complications, limiting net clinical benefit to settings with expert shock teams and careful patient selection.
weaknesses: Highly selected population excluding comatose post-arrest patients

sections.authors_conclusion: Routine Impella CP support in selected infarct-related cardiogenic shock was associated with improved survival at 180 days, but with a substantial increase in major harms, shifting practice from 'device enthusiasm' to 'device plus selection plus systems'.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This trial changes practice by providing evidence that Impella CP can improve survival in carefully selected patients, but mandates rigorous patient selection, procedural expertise, and integrated shock systems to mitigate harm.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Patients with STEMI-related cardiogenic shock without coma after OHCA, treated in high-volume centres with shock teams.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean Impella CP should be used routinely in all cardiogenic shock; benefit-risk profile is unfavourable in less selected populations or centres without expertise.
implementation_caveats: Requires immediate access to large-bore access and catheter lab
High risk of severe bleeding and renal failure necessitates careful monitoring and management
Benefit likely depends on early placement and protocolised support duration

controversies.notes: Mortality reduction (HR 0.74) but composite safety endpoint RR 4.74, severe bleeding 20.1% vs 3.4%, raising questions about net clinical benefit in broader populations.
Exclusion of comatose post-OHCA patients (435 of 851 excluded) limits applicability; benefit may be concentrated in those without hypoxic brain injury.

controversies.topic: Timing of support relative to PCI
controversies.notes: Substantial proportion randomised after revascularisation; unclear if benefit reflects post-PCI support rather than pre-PCI unloading; subgroup analysis showed no interaction.
Early VA-ECMO in infarct-related shock has not shown survival advantage and increases complications, reinforcing that modality and selection matter.
Recent meta-analysis including DanGer Shock reported mortality reduction signals for microaxial pumps alongside increased bleeding/vascular complications.

unresolved_questions: Optimal patient selection criteria to maximise benefit and minimise harm
Cost-effectiveness of routine Impella CP strategy
Effect in non-STEMI shock and mixed shock aetiologies
Impact of timing of device placement relative to PCI

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In selected STEMI-related cardiogenic shock, routine Impella CP reduced 180-day mortality but doubled severe bleeding and increased renal-replacement therapy, making patient selection and shock-team expertise essential.
